content: Caesarean section involves creating an incision in the abdominal wall and the uterine muscle to deliver the baby. In some cases, delivery during a caesarean section can be challenging, potentially leading to complications for both the mother and the infant. Techniques to assist delivery during such difficult caesarean births include the use of vacuum or forceps extraction, manual delivery with fundal pressure, or medications that relax the uterus (tocolytic agents). When the fetal head is deeply impacted, particularly after prolonged obstructed labor, the surgeon may employ either reverse breech extraction or the head-pushing technique to facilitate delivery. The objective of this review was to compare the use of tocolytic agents (either routinely or selectively) versus no tocolysis or placebo, as well as to compare different methods of fetal extraction during caesarean section. The outcomes of interest included infant birth trauma, maternal complications (such as postpartum hemorrhage requiring blood transfusion), and long-term infant and childhood morbidity. The review included seven randomized controlled trials involving 582 women undergoing caesarean section. The quality of the included trials varied, with some studies lacking adequate descriptions of allocation or randomization methods. The findings were categorized into three main comparisons: 1. Tocolysis versus no tocolysis: One randomized trial involving 97 women was included. Birth trauma was not reported in this study. No maternal side effects were observed in either the nitroglycerin (tocolytic) or placebo groups. No other maternal or infant health outcomes were reported. 2. Reverse breech extraction versus head-pushing for deeply impacted fetal head at full dilation: Four randomized trials involving 357 women were included. Birth trauma, the primary outcome, was reported in three trials, with no significant difference between the two techniques (risk ratio [RR] 1.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 5.73). Secondary outcomes showed that reverse breech extraction was associated with: A lower rate of endometritis (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.05). A significantly reduced risk of uterine incision extension (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.40). A significant reduction in mean blood loss (mean difference [MD] -294.92 mL, 95% CI -493.25 to -96.59). Fewer neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) or special care nursery (SCN) admissions (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.22). No differences were observed between the two techniques for other secondary outcomes, such as blood loss >500 mL, blood transfusion, wound infection, mean hospital stay, or Apgar scores. Reverse breech extraction was associated with a shorter operative time, which may reflect easier delivery, reduced tissue trauma, and consequently less blood loss. However, due to significant heterogeneity between trials, the exact magnitude of differences in blood loss, operative time, or hospital stay could not be determined. 3. Instrumental (vacuum or forceps) versus manual extraction at elective caesarean section: Two randomized trials involving 128 women were included. Only one trial reported maternal and infant health outcomes as specified in this review. Birth trauma was reported as an outcome, but no cases of birth trauma occurred in either group. No significant differences were found in mean hemoglobin (Hb) drop between groups (MD 0.03, 95% CI -0.53 to 0.59) or in the rate of uterine incision extension (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.13 to 3.73). Conclusions: There is currently insufficient evidence from randomized trials to definitively support or refute the routine or selective use of tocolytic agents or instrumental methods to facilitate delivery during difficult caesarean sections. Limited evidence suggests that reverse breech extraction may improve maternal and neonatal outcomes, although no difference was observed in the primary outcome of infant birth trauma. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to address these questions and provide more robust evidence.
